steps.body: One chapter left to close Grade 7 geometry: putting it all together. Scale drawings convert, circles measure, angle facts become equations, side lengths decide triangles, and cuts reveal cross-sections.

widget.prompt: On a 1 cm = 2 m plan, a circular fountain has a drawing radius of 3 cm. What is its REAL radius, in meters?

choices.label: 6 m
choices.feedback: The scale chain is exact: 3 × 2 = 6 m.

choices.label: 3 m
choices.feedback: That's the drawing radius — convert with the scale: 3 × 2 = 6 m.

choices.label: 12 m
choices.feedback: That doubled twice (or used the diameter) — the radius converts once: 3 × 2 = 6 m.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Drawing → real multiplies by the scale: 3 × 2 = 6 m.
widget.successFeedback: The scale chain is exact: 3 × 2 = 6 m.

predict.prompt: Drawing radius 3 cm on a 1 cm = 2 m plan (real radius 6 m). Is the REAL area just 2 × the drawing's area number?

options.label: Areas don't scale with the plan

predict.reveal: Lengths scale ×2 but areas ×4: the drawing's 9π becomes a real 36π. Converting the radius FIRST (3 cm → 6 m, then πr²) dodges the trap automatically — scale the length, then square.

steps.body: Skills chain together. That 6 m radius feeds straight into the circle formulas: circumference C = 2π × 6 = 12π meters of fence, area A = π × 6² = 36π square meters of water.

widget.prompt: The real fountain has radius 6 m. How much fencing wraps around it, as a number times π (meters)?

choices.label: 36π m
choices.feedback: That's r² (the AREA) — fencing follows the circumference: 2 × 6 = 12π.

choices.label: 6π m
choices.feedback: That's the radius — C = 2πr doubles it: 12π.

widget.prompt: The same fountain (radius 6 m): how much water surface does it hold, as a number times π (square meters)?

choices.label: 12π m²
choices.feedback: That's 2r (the circumference) — area SQUARES the radius: 6² = 36π.

explanationVariants: The two path angles fill a straight line: x + 2x = 180 → 3x = 180 → x = 60.

widget.prompt: Two garden paths meet the fountain's edge, making angles x and 2x on a straight line. Solve for x (in degrees).

commonAngles.feedback: That solved 2x = 180 — combine BOTH terms: 3x = 180, so x = 60.
A straight line holds 180°, not 90°: 3x = 180, x = 60.

widget.successFeedback: The two parts now fill the straight line: 60° + 120° = 180°.

explanationVariants: 7 + 8 = 15 beats 12, so the three beams close into a triangle.

widget.prompt: A triangular trellis needs beams of 7, 8, and 12 feet. Will they form a triangle?

choices.label: Yes — 7 + 8 = 15 beats 12
choices.feedback: Right — the shorter pair out-reaches the longest beam, so the frame closes.

choices.label: No — 12 is too long
choices.feedback: Check the sum: 7 + 8 = 15 > 12, so the beams DO close into a triangle.

choices.label: No — the sides differ
choices.feedback: Different sides are fine — 7 + 8 > 12 passes the triangle test.

choices.label: Only if 12 is the base
choices.feedback: Position doesn't matter — 7 + 8 > 12 works regardless of which beam is the base.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Compare 7 + 8 with 12. The shorter pair must strictly out-reach the longest beam.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the shorter pair out-reaches the longest beam, so the frame closes.

explanationVariants: Real radius: 2 × 2 = 4 m. Area: π × 4² = 16π m².

widget.prompt: A second fountain is 2 cm in radius on the 1 cm = 2 m plan. What is its REAL area, as a number times π (square meters)?

choices.label: 16π m²
choices.feedback: The real radius is 4 m, and 4² = 16, so the area is 16π m².

choices.label: 4π m²
choices.feedback: That's the real radius (2 × 2 = 4 m) — now SQUARE it for area: 16π.

choices.label: 8π m²
choices.feedback: That's the circumference (2 × 4) — area squares the radius: 4² = 16π.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Real radius: 2 × 2 = 4 m. A = πr² = 16π m².
widget.successFeedback: The real radius is 4 m, and 4² = 16, so the area is 16π m².

hints: Convert the radius to real meters first: 2 cm × 2 m per cm.
Real radius = 4 m. Area squares it.

steps.body: Scale, circles, angles, triangles, and slices — Grade 7 geometry, complete.
takeaways: Convert with the scale first, then apply circle formulas.
Angle facts become equations; side sums decide triangles.
You now hold every 7.G tool — and the πr² behind Grade 8's volumes.
steps.teaser: That completes Grade 7 Geometry — and with it, all five Grade 7 domains.

concept.body: Chain the skills: convert lengths with the scale FIRST (drawing → real multiplies), then use the circle formulas — C = 2πr doubles the radius, A = πr² squares it.
